![Tile matrix titled Cholesterol's link to death looks different at different ages. Each tile compares the death rate of US adults in one total cholesterol group with adults at 180 to 199 mg/dL, set at 1.00. Before taking age and sex into account, adults at 240+ mg/dL had a 27% higher death rate (1.27); after, the estimate was 1.00, showing no clear difference. Within age groups, the 240+ estimate was 1.42 for ages 18 to 49 (based on 128 deaths and sensitive to survey weighting), 1.02 for ages 50 to 69, and 0.91 for ages 70 and over. Below 160 mg/dL, death rates were higher in every row, from 1.19 to 1.46; treatment and underlying illness were not measured. Average age rose from 42 in the lowest cholesterol group to 51 in the highest. Data: NHANES 1999 to 2018 linked to NCHS mortality records through 2019.](tt_2026_46.png){#fig-1}

::: {.key-takeaways}
[Key takeaways]{.key-takeaways-label}

- Age matters when comparing cholesterol groups. Adults at 240+ mg/dL averaged 51 years old, versus 46 in the comparison group, and the apparent excess mortality hazard was no longer detectable after adjusting for age and sex.
- In survey-weighted Cox models of 52,634 adults and 7,632 deaths, the hazard ratio at 240+ mg/dL changed from 1.27 (95% CI 1.14–1.40) to 1.00 (0.90–1.11). The association also differed across age groups (interaction p = 0.00025).
- Cholesterol below 160 mg/dL was associated with higher mortality hazard in all three age groups, but underlying illness and cholesterol-lowering treatment could contribute to this pattern. The dataset lacks statin use, smoking and baseline illness; the 18–49 high-cholesterol estimate is sensitive to survey weighting. Individual comparisons were not adjusted for multiple testing.
:::

#### [2. Read in the Data]{.smallcaps}

```{r}
#| label: read
#| include: true
#| eval: true
#| warning: false

### |- figure settings ----
fig_w    <- 12
fig_h    <- 7.5
fig_dpi  <- 320
out_file <- "2026/Week_46/2026_46.png"

### |- fonts ----
setup_fonts()
fonts <- get_font_families()
title_family <- fonts$title_1
title_size   <- 28


## 2. READ IN THE DATA ----
## Read every field as character with no NA tokens; restore numbers column by column.
read_chr <- function(path) {
  read_csv(path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), na = character(), show_col_types = FALSE)
}

tt_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-11-17/"
cm_raw <- read_chr(paste0(tt_url, "cholesterol_mortality.csv"))
est_raw <- read_chr(here::here("data/TidyTuesday/2026/tt_2026_46_estimates.csv"))

```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
##### Expand for the decision record (how the estimates were made)

`tt_2026_46_decision_record.R` holds the full analysis behind the chart:

- Data checks: the derived columns recomputed, the meaning of missing values, follow-up length by cycle, and the sample reconciled with Li, Fu & Zhang (2025).
- Survey weights: 2/10 × WTMEC4YR for 1999–2002 and 1/10 × WTMEC2YR for 2003–2018, as recommended for pooled NHANES cycles.
- Models: crude and age- and sex-adjusted Cox models, robustness checks (age specification, bins, early deaths, weighting), age-group results, and interaction tests.
- Export: the estimates the chart displays, written to `tt_2026_46_estimates.csv`.

To reproduce: run the decision record first (it downloads the two NHANES demographic files from the CDC), then `2026_46.R`.
:::

#### [4. Tidy Data]{.smallcaps}

```{r}
#| label: tidy
#| warning: false

### |- analysis population ----
cm <- cm_raw |>
  mutate(across(c(total_chol, hdl, died), \(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(na_if(x, "NA")))))
an <- cm |> filter(!is.na(total_chol), !is.na(hdl), hdl <= 140)
n_adults <- nrow(an)
n_deaths <- sum(an$died)

### |- estimates ----
bins_raw <- c("<160", "160-179", "180-199", "200-219", "220-239", "240+")
bins_show <- c("Below 160", "160–179", "180–199", "200–219", "220–239", "240+")

est <- est_raw |>
  mutate(
    across(c(value, lo, hi, deaths), \(x) as.numeric(na_if(x, ""))),
    col = match(bin, bins_raw)
  )

hr <- est |> filter(kind == "hr_weighted")

### |- matrix layout: rows top to bottom = the reading order ----
## groups (1), (2), (3) are separated by wider gaps than rows within a group, so the
## matrix reads as three steps, not one heatmap
row_y <- c(crude_all = 6.3, adj_all = 4.95, adj_18_49 = 3.3, adj_50_69 = 2.3, adj_70p = 1.3)

cells <- hr |>
  mutate(
    y = unname(row_y[row_key]),
    status = case_when(
      bin == "180-199" ~ "ref",
      lo > 1 ~ "higher",
      hi < 1 ~ "lower",
      TRUE ~ "unclear"
    ),
    lab_hr = if_else(status == "ref", "1.00", sprintf("%.2f", value)),
    lab_ci = case_when(
      status == "ref" & row_key == "crude_all" ~ "comparison",
      status == "ref" ~ "",
      TRUE ~ sprintf("%.2f–%.2f", lo, hi)
    ),
    y_hr = if_else(lab_ci == "", y, y + 0.13)
  )

### |- numbers quoted in copy (all from the export) ----
pick <- function(key, b, k = "hr_weighted") est |> filter(kind == k, row_key == key, bin == b)
crude_240 <- pick("crude_all", "240+")
adj_240 <- pick("adj_all", "240+")
young_240 <- pick("adj_18_49", "240+")
young_unw <- pick("adj_18_49", "240+", "hr_unweighted")
mean_age <- est |>
  filter(kind == "mean_age_weighted") |>
  arrange(col)

pct_crude <- round((crude_240$value - 1) * 100)
dip <- pick("adj_50_69", "200-219")
pct_dip <- round((1 - dip$value) * 100)
age_240 <- mean_age$value[mean_age$bin == "240+"]
age_ref <- mean_age$value[mean_age$bin == "180-199"]
```

### |- plot aesthetics ----

subtitle_text <- glue(
  "Each tile compares the death rate of US adults in one cholesterol group with adults at 180–199 mg/dL (1.00).<br>",
  "{sprintf('%.2f', crude_240$value)} means a {pct_crude}% higher death rate; ",

## three caption lines
caption_lines <- c(
  "Hazard ratios with 95% intervals, survey-weighted Cox models (CDC 20-year exam weights) stratified by NHANES cycle; rows 2–5 adjusted for age and sex.",
  glue(
    "{comma(n_adults)} adults, {comma(n_deaths)} deaths, follow-up through 2019; HDL over 140 mg/dL excluded. ",
    "Colour marks intervals entirely above or below 1.00."

)

caption_text <- paste0(

  create_social_caption(
    tt_year = 2026,

### |- plot theme ----

#### [6. Plot]{.smallcaps}

```{r}
#| label: plot
#| warning: false


### |- matrix ----
tile_w <- 0.94
tile_h <- 0.86
x_lab  <- 0.42        
x_note <- 6.62       

row_labels <- tibble(
    y     = unname(row_y),
    main  = c("(1)  All adults", "(2)  All adults", "Ages 18–49", "Ages 50–69", "Ages 70+"),
    sub   = c("before taking age and sex into account", "taking age and sex into account", "", "", "")
)

### |- main plot ----
p <- ggplot(cells) +
  # Geoms
  geom_tile(aes(x = col, y = y, fill = status), width = tile_w, height = tile_h, color = NA) +
  geom_tile(
    data = filter(cells, status %in% c("unclear", "ref")),
    aes(x = col, y = y), width = tile_w, height = tile_h,
    fill = NA, color = col_outline, linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = col, y = y_hr, label = lab_hr,
      color = if_else(status %in% c("higher", "lower"), "on_dark", "on_light")
    ),
    family = fonts$text, fontface = "bold", size = 4.1
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = col, y = y - 0.19, label = lab_ci,
      color = if_else(status %in% c("higher", "lower"), "on_dark", "on_light")
    ),
    family = fonts$caption, size = 2.5
  ) +
  # column headers
  annotate("text",
    x = 1:6, y = 7.4, label = bins_show,
    family = fonts$text, fontface = "bold", size = 3.3, color = col_ink
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0.53, y = 7.85, hjust = 0, label = "Total cholesterol, mg/dL",
    family = fonts$text, size = 3.1, color = col_muted
  ) +
  # row labels
  geom_text(
    data = row_labels, aes(x = x_lab, y = y + if_else(sub == "", 0, 0.12), label = main),
    hjust = 1, family = fonts$text, fontface = "bold", size = 3.3, color = col_ink
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = filter(row_labels, sub != ""), aes(x = x_lab, y = y - 0.2, label = sub),
    hjust = 1, family = fonts$text, size = 2.9, color = col_muted
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = x_lab, y = 4.18, hjust = 1, label = "(3)  By age group",
    family = fonts$text, fontface = "bold", size = 3.3, color = col_ink
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = x_lab, y = 3.85, hjust = 1, label = "taking age and sex into account",
    family = fonts$text, size = 2.9, color = col_muted
  ) +
  # context row: mean age (subordinate)
  annotate("text",
    x = 1:6, y = 6.95, label = round(mean_age$value),
    family = fonts$caption, size = 3, color = col_muted
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = x_lab, y = 6.95, hjust = 1, label = "Average age",
    family = fonts$text, size = 2.9, color = col_muted
  ) +
  # notes at the mark: one per step on the right, the low-end caveat below
  annotate("text",
    x = x_note, y = row_y[["crude_all"]], hjust = 0, label = cue_crude,
    family = fonts$text, size = 2.8, color = col_ink, lineheight = 1.15
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = x_note, y = row_y[["adj_all"]], hjust = 0, label = note_adj,
    family = fonts$text, size = 2.8, color = col_ink, lineheight = 1.15
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = x_note, y = row_y[["adj_18_49"]], hjust = 0, label = note_young,
    family = fonts$text, size = 2.8, color = col_ink, lineheight = 1.15
  ) +
  annotate("segment",
    x = 1 - tile_w / 2, xend = 1 + tile_w / 2, y = 0.73, yend = 0.73,
    color = col_ink, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 1 - tile_w / 2, y = 0.61, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, label = note_low,
    family = fonts$text, size = 2.8, color = col_ink, lineheight = 1.15
  ) +
  # Scales
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(higher = col_higher, lower = col_lower, unclear = col_unclear, ref = col_ref),
    breaks = c("higher", "lower", "unclear"),
    labels = c("Higher death rate", "Lower death rate", "No clear difference")
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(on_dark = "#FFFFFF", on_light = col_ink), guide = "none") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(color = col_outline, linewidth = 0.3))) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-2.6, 9.6), expand = expansion(0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.15, 8.05), expand = expansion(0)) +
  # Labs
  labs(title = title_text, subtitle = subtitle_text, caption = caption_text)
```

#### [10. References]{.smallcaps}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
##### Expand for References

**Primary Data (TidyTuesday):** 1. TidyTuesday `r current_year` Week `r current_week`: `r create_link("Cholesterol and Mortality in US Adults", "https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-11-17")`, curated by Tony Galvan. - One row per adult: total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, triglycerides, two ratios, age, sex, race, survey design columns and mortality status. 52,678 adults from ten NHANES cycles (1999–2018). - The curation script uses the two-year exam weight (WTMEC2YR) for every cycle and has no fasting-subsample weight. The data dictionary reverses the age top-codes: NHANES codes ages 85 and over as 85 in 1999–2006 and ages 80 and over as 80 from 2007. It also says to divide weights by the number of cycles, which is not the CDC rule for 1999–2002. - LDL and triglycerides come from the fasting subsample (about half the adults) and are not used.

**Source Data:** 2. National Center for Health Statistics. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1999–2018, linked to the `r create_link("2019 Public-Use Linked Mortality Files", "https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm")` (follow-up through December 31, 2019). - The public-use mortality files are perturbed to protect participants' identities, so some follow-up times and causes of death are synthetic. This matters more for cause-specific analyses, which the chart does not use.

**Enrichment Data:** 3. National Center for Health Statistics. `r create_link("NHANES 1999–2000 Demographics (DEMO)", "https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhanes/public/1999/datafiles/DEMO.htm")` and 2001–2002 (DEMO_B): four-year exam weights (WTMEC4YR), joined by SEQN. - Pooled 20-year weights follow the `r create_link("NHANES weighting tutorial", "https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/default.aspx")`: 2/10 × WTMEC4YR for 1999–2002, 1/10 × WTMEC2YR for 2003–2018. The file's survey_weight matches WTMEC2YR exactly for 1999–2002. - Population represented: 212.5 million adults (212.0 million with the dictionary's simpler rule).

**Analysis Script:** 4. `r create_link("tt_2026_46_decision_record.R", "https://github.com/poncest/tidytuesday/tree/main/2026/Week_46")`: data checks, weight rebuild, survey-weighted Cox models (`survey::svycoxph()`), robustness checks and interaction tests. It writes `tt_2026_46_estimates.csv`, which the chart reads.

**Prior Coverage:** 5. Li S, Fu Z, Zhang W (2025). `r create_link("Association of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol with all-cause and cause-specific mortality in the general population: insights from NHANES 1999–2018", "https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22251-z")`. BMC Public Health 25:1123. Same NHANES cycles, HDL only, with U-shaped curves and forest plots; this chart avoids both designs. Their 51,235 adults and 7,602 deaths sit close to this analysis's 52,634 and 7,632. Most of the gap is the pregnant participants they excluded, whom this file cannot identify. 6. Yi SW, Yi JJ, Ohrr H (2019). `r create_link("Total cholesterol and all-cause mortality by sex and age: a prospective cohort study among 12.8 million adults", "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-38461-y")`. Scientific Reports 9:1596. The Korean U-curve the TidyTuesday readme cites. 7. Zhou D et al. (2022). `r create_link("The effect of total cholesterol/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio on mortality risk in the general population", "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9797665")`. The ratio angle on NHANES was already published, so it was not used here. 8. `r create_link("Non-HDL cholesterol and mortality by age, NHANES (Frontiers in Nutrition, 2025)", "https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1591705/epub")`. Reports age differences for non-HDL cholesterol; the three age bands here follow its split (under 50, 50–69, 70+).

**Analysis Frame:** - **Population:** 52,634 of 52,678 adults with total cholesterol and HDL measured, excluding HDL above 140 mg/dL, as in Li et al.; 7,632 deaths. - **Measure:** hazard ratios (death rates relative to adults at 180–199 mg/dL) from survey-weighted Cox models stratified by NHANES cycle, because follow-up runs from about 2 to 20 years depending on cycle. Raw "share who died" is never compared across groups. - **Before and after:** at 240+ mg/dL, 1.27 (1.14–1.40) before adjustment; 1.27 adjusting for sex alone; 0.95 (0.86–1.06) adjusting for age alone; 1.00 (0.90–1.11) adjusting for age and sex. Below 160 mg/dL: 1.19, then 1.35. Average age rises from 42 (below 160) to 51 (240+), weighted. - **Robustness of the 240+ result:** 0.96 to 1.05 under quadratic age, age bands, age as the time scale, excluding 1999–2002, bins shifted by 10 mg/dL, and men and women separately. - **Age groups:** at 240+, ages 18–49 1.42 (1.07–1.89), 50–69 1.02 (0.85–1.22), 70+ 0.91 (0.80–1.04). Below 160 mg/dL, higher in every group (1.46, 1.41, 1.27). The pattern differs by age group (interaction test, p = 0.00025). - **Claim limits:** the individual cholesterol-group comparisons are exploratory and were not adjusted for multiple testing; the age-dependent pattern overall rests on the interaction test, so individual tiles (such as the two lower cells at ages 50–69) should be read cautiously. The 18–49 estimate at 240+ is based on 128 deaths and is sensitive to survey weighting (1.26, 0.99–1.60, without weights). Statin use, smoking and illness at the exam are not in the data, so the chart shows associations only, not what raising or lowering cholesterol would do. - **Not used:** the cholesterol ratios (already published); cause of death (low cholesterol and heart-disease deaths is likely confounded by statin treatment, which isn't measured); how much cholesterol adds to predicting death beyond age and sex (0.0008 to 0.0019 in concordance, too small to chart); excluding early deaths (the low-cholesterol excess goes 1.35 → 1.31 → 1.22 at 0, 2 and 5 years, with overlapping intervals; a robustness check, not a finding); LDL and triglycerides (fasting subsample, no fasting weight). - **Scope:** observational and descriptive of associations in US adults, 1999–2018; no clinical or causal claim.
:::


#### [11. Custom Functions Documentation]{.smallcaps}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
##### 📦 Custom Helper Functions

This analysis uses custom functions from my personal module library for efficiency and consistency across projects.

**Functions Used:**

-   **`fonts.R`**: `setup_fonts()`, `get_font_families()` - Font management with showtext
-   **`social_icons.R`**: `create_social_caption()` - Generates formatted social media captions
-   **`base_theme.R`**: `create_base_theme()`, `extend_weekly_theme()`, `get_theme_colors()` - Custom ggplot2 themes

**Why custom functions?**\
